newsitem.title: USA: Shuttle-deployed telescope ready for action.
newsitem.headline: Shuttle-deployed telescope ready for action.

text.p: A small free-flying telescope was readied to look deep into space, seeking the secrets of the stars, while the crew of space shuttle Columbia on Wednesday settled into their orbital work routine.
Columbia's five astronauts had a relatively quiet day following their Tuesday blastoff and release of a U.S.-German orbiting observatory.
The Orfeus-Spas telescope was set free from the mechanical grip of Columbia's robot arm on Tuesday. It was the first major task of the 16-day mission.
Scientists controlling the telescope from the Kennedy Space Centre said they ran into minor difficulty aligning the instrument but expected to start observations as planned on Wednesday night.
"That alignment process is not a problem, it is a normal part of the calibration," mission scientist Ronald Polidan told a news conference.

The orbiting observatory's 1-metre ultraviolet telescope will be trained on the interstellar gases that lie between the stars. This mysterious matter forms the building blocks of stars and is also shed by stars as they die.

"By understanding these apparently arcane questions of interstellar gases we're learning a little bit about the eventual future of our very own solar system, as well as the general life cycle of birth and death in the galaxy," said Mark Hurwitz, one of the project's scientists.
The Orfeus-Spas will fly free of Columbia for nearly two weeks before being picked up again by the shuttle's robot arm.

A second satellite, the saucer-like Wake Shield Facility, will be deployed from Columbia on Friday and retrieved three days later. The stainless steel spacecraft will employ the vacuum of space to manufacture ultra-pure semi-conductors for the electronics industry.

The astronauts got an extra hour in bed on Wednesday to make up for their late night deploying the Orfeus-Spas. They were awakened by "I can see for miles" by The Who, broadcast up to the shuttle by mission control.

They spent their second day in orbit setting up medical research experiments and trying out a prototype positioning system which may be used by future space crews to assist in orbital rendezvous and docking manoeuvres.
The crew included Story Musgrave, 61, who was the oldest person to orbit the Earth. NASA officials told Musgrave his sixth venture into space will be his last.

The astronauts were not due back on earth until Dec. 5 and will miss the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday. They will, however, get NASA's version of the traditional family meal -- irradiated turkey steaks are on the shuttle menu.
